domain: Software Licensing / Copyright Law / Open Source Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the GNU General Public License's 'derivative work' trigger clause, focusing on the unresolved interpretive contest over whether linking (static or dynamic) creates a derivative work requiring source disclosure. The FSF broad copyleft reading grounds authority in license intent to propagate freedom; the narrow linking-permissive reading grounds authority in statutory copyright's idea/expression distinction.

key_entities: Free Software Foundation (FSF) — license author, interpretive authority claimant
GNU General Public License v2/v3 — kernel text with 'work based on the Program' trigger
Linking operation — technical act of combining program modules (static/dynamic/header)
Statutory copyright law — U.S. Copyright Act §106 derivative work doctrine
Proprietary software vendors — entities seeking to avoid copyleft propagation
Downstream users — beneficiaries of source availability under broad reading, victims of unavailability under narrow
key_tensions: License intent (FSF's propagation goal) vs statutory text (copyright's idea/expression line)
Technical coupling (linking as mere aggregation vs derivative creation)
key_claims: FSF: Dynamic linking creates a derivative work triggering GPL obligations (grounded in license intent)
Narrow reading: Linking is aggregation not derivation (grounded in copyright statute)
No binding U.S. appellate precedent directly resolves GPL linking scope
LGPL exists as FSF's own accommodation of narrow-reading concerns (library exception)
key_mechanisms: Copyleft propagation — GPL §2(b) obligation to disclose source for derivative works
Linking operation — technical coupling via symbol resolution at compile or runtime
Authority vacuum — absence of binding precedent leaves interpretive contest open
key_absences: Judicial resolution — Oracle v. Google addressed API copyrightability but not GPL linking
AGPL network-trigger clause — not present in base GPL, separate axis for SaaS loophole

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The GPL's 'work based on the Program' clause as the shared commitment all parties argue about — FSF reads it as triggered by linking (broad), statutory-copyright readers limit it to modifications (narrow)
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: FSF claims interpretive authority via authorship and intent; narrow readers ground authority in statutory copyright as the controlling legal framework

readings.commitment: Linking (even dynamic) creates a derivative work under GPL, triggering source disclosure obligation
readings.authority_grounding: License author intent (FSF); propagation of software freedom as telos
readings.expected_structural_delta: Rope pulling dependent code into commons; downstream users gain source access; proprietary vendors face compliance cost or avoidance

readings.commitment: Linking is aggregation not derivation; only modifications to GPL code trigger obligations
readings.authority_grounding: Statutory copyright (17 USC §106); idea/expression distinction; derivative work requires expression copying
readings.expected_structural_delta: Wall protecting proprietary modules; users of those modules lose source-availability guarantee; FSF's propagation goal frustrated

readings.commitment: Clean API boundaries constitute non-derivative aggregation even with tight coupling
readings.authority_grounding: Technical pragmatism; Oracle v. Google fair use precedent (APIs non-copyrightable); plugin architecture norms
readings.expected_structural_delta: Scaffold allowing modular architecture with mixed licensing; beneficiaries are ecosystem integrators; victims are users expecting full-stack source under broad reading

axiom_contradictions.basis: No single coherent framework can hold both that linking creates a derivative work (broad) and that linking is mere aggregation (narrow) — accepting statutory copyright's idea/expression line as controlling requires rejecting FSF's intent-based authority over derivative-work scope

omegas.source: Deferred axis: precedent_vacuum; Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)

omegas.description: AGPL (Affero GPL) adds network-use trigger for SaaS loophole — separate kernel from linking contest, but structurally coupled. Is AGPL's existence evidence that base GPL linking scope is intentionally narrow (FSF adding explicit trigger where implicit failed)?
omegas.source: Absence Inventory: AGPL not present in base GPL

omegas.description: Does Oracle v. Google (API copyrightability rejected, fair use for reimplementation) collapse interface_boundary_reading into narrow_linking_permissive_reading, or does it scaffold a distinct third position? Post-2021 enforcement patterns unclear.

Linux kernel explicitly permits proprietary modules via MODULE_LICENSE tag and Torvalds' public statements — is this a fourth reading (authority-by-benevolent-dictator) or a piton eroding broad_copyleft_reading's force in the most prominent GPL ecosystem?
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory); entity not extracted but structurally relevant

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel structure confirmed: three readings with mutually exclusive axioms, distinct authority groundings, and different beneficiary/victim sets. Precedent vacuum and LGPL deferred as lower-yield supporting evidence. AGPL and Linux kernel MODULE_LICENSE identified as omega-level coupling points for future analysis.
